<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par97 />On the connective forms {{GHGheb|text=שְׁבַע}}, {{GHGheb|text=תְּשַׁע}}, cf. the analogous forms in {{GHGpar|93|h}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|97|c}}
The other Semitic languages also exhibit the same peculiarity in the external differentiation of the numerals from 3 to 10 as regards gender. The fem. form of the numeral abstracts is only rarely found in connexion with feminine nouns,<ref>In the vulgar dialects of Arabic, and in Ethiopic, the feminine form of the numeral is by far the more common. This form appears also in Hebrew, when the number is regarded in the abstract, as in the multiplicatives (see {{GHGpar|97|h}}).</ref> e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת נָשִׁים}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=7|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=10|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=7|verse=2}} {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>th.}}; probably also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=17|verse=11}}, where we should read with Dillmann {{GHGheb|text=שׁ׳ הַגָּפּוֹת}}. In apposition, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=3|verse=9}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=4|verse=2|hidebook=1}}, cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=23}}. From what was said above, under ''a'', it follows that these cases are not a return to original usage, but only an intrusion of the form used before masculines into the sphere of the feminine. Conversely in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=38|verse=24}} {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשׁ חֳדָשִׁים}} (but in the Samaritan {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת}}).—For {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָה|translate=seven}}, there occurs in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=42|verse=13}} the strange form {{GHGheb|text=שִׁבְעָ֫נָה}}, according to Ewald [{{GHGcite|title=Ausführl, Lehrb.}}<sup>8</sup>, {{GHGpar|269|b}}] an old feminine substantive (German ''ein Siebend'', ''a set of seven''), but more probably a scribal error.

{{GHGmargin-letter|97|d}}
'''2.''' The numerals from 11 to 19 are formed by placing the units, without the ''copula'', before the number ten (in the form {{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂר}} masc., {{GHGheb|text=עֶשְׂרֵה}} fem.), but without the two words being joined into one. As was said above, under ''a'', and as is proved by the use of {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד}}, {{GHGheb|text=אַחַת}} in the numeral 11, the feminine numerals from 13 to 19 are to be regarded as ''construct'' forms in a genitive connexion. The connective forms of the masculine abstracts, like {{GHGheb|text=שְׁל֫שֶׁת}}, &c., are not admitted in combination with {{GHGheb|text=עָשָׂר}}, since they are merely in apposition, and not in a genitive relation (see the rare exceptions at the end of ''e''). On the other hand {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} in the numeral 12 are undoubtedly true ''constructs'', like {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד}} and the fem. numerals 13–19. But instead of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=3|verse=12}} and four other places) and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=4|verse=8}} and three times in Ezek.), we generally find {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}} and {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּים}}. Two explanations have been given of these forms: (1) that the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} really intends {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}, in the ''absol. st.'', which was first introduced in the case of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנַ֫יִם}}, on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=עֲשָׂרָה}}, &c., and then extended to {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}}; the Masora, however, required {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵי}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּי}} (but see below), and therefore pointed {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שׁתֵּים}} as a ''Q<sup>e</sup>rê perpetuum'' (see § 17).—(2) that the ''absolute'' forms {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵ֫יִם}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתַּ֫יִם}} (introduced on the analogy of {{GHGheb|text=שְׁלשָׁה}}, &c.) were contracted to {{GHGheb|text=שְׁנֵים}}, {{GHGheb|text=שְׁתֵּים}} to facilitate the pronunciation of the duals when closely<section end=par97 /><noinclude>
